questions.topic: ACE inhibitors and renal artery stenosis
questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with long-standing hypertension, peripheral artery disease, and a 60-pack-year smoking history has bruits heard over both flanks. He is started on lisinopril. One week later his serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL. Renal artery imaging shows severe atherosclerotic narrowing of both renal arteries.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the decrease in this patient's glomerular filtration rate?

options.text: Loss of angiotensin II-mediated constriction of the efferent arterioles
Angiotensin II-mediated constriction of the afferent arterioles
Bradykinin-mediated injury to the proximal tubule

questions.explanation: Answer: loss of efferent arteriolar constriction. Why: when both renal arteries are narrowed (or the only kidney's artery is narrowed), blood flow into the glomerulus is low, and the kidney keeps filtering by using angiotensin II to squeeze the efferent (outflow) arteriole, which holds glomerular pressure up. GFR (glomerular filtration rate) becomes dependent on that efferent tone. An ACE inhibitor removes angiotensin II, the efferent arteriole relaxes, glomerular pressure falls, and GFR drops, so creatinine rises. This is why a creatinine jump after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB should raise suspicion for bilateral renal artery stenosis.

whyWrong.b: ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II, and angiotensin II mainly constricts the efferent, not the afferent, arteriole.
whyWrong.c: Allergic interstitial nephritis comes with fever, rash, or urine eosinophils and is not explained by bilateral renal artery narrowing.
whyWrong.d: Extra bradykinin explains ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema, not a hemodynamic drop in GFR.
whyWrong.e: ACE inhibitors lower aldosterone, and aldosterone would not lower GFR.

sources.title: StatPearls: Physiology, Renal Blood Flow and Filtration

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease with proteinuria is started on empagliflozin. Three months later his hemoglobin A1c has decreased, and he has had one episode of genital yeast infection. Urinalysis shows marked glucosuria despite a blood glucose of 140 mg/dL.
questions.leadIn: This drug acts on a transporter located in which part of the nephron?

options.text: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

questions.explanation: Answer: proximal convoluted tubule. Why: empagliflozin blocks the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) in the proximal tubule, so glucose that was filtered is not taken back and is lost in urine (glucosuria). More sodium then reaches the distal nephron, which triggers tubuloglomerular feedback: the afferent arteriole constricts and pressure inside the glomerulus falls. Lower glomerular pressure is the main way SGLT2 inhibitors protect the kidney. Key side effects are genital yeast infections, urinary tract infections, volume depletion, and euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis.

whyWrong.b: The thick ascending limb holds the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, the target of loop diuretics like furosemide.
whyWrong.c: The distal convoluted tubule holds the Na-Cl cotransporter, the target of thiazide diuretics.
whyWrong.d: Principal cells hold ENaC sodium channels and aldosterone receptors, targets of amiloride and spironolactone.
whyWrong.e: The glomerulus filters glucose but does not reabsorb it; there is no glucose transporter drug target there.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with an LDL cholesterol of 190 mg/dL is started on atorvastatin. Eight weeks later his LDL cholesterol has fallen to 95 mg/dL. He reports mild muscle aches.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the main reason this drug lowered his plasma LDL cholesterol?

options.text: Increased hepatic LDL receptor expression after reduced hepatic cholesterol synthesis
Binding of bile acids in the intestine
Inhibition of the intestinal cholesterol transporter NPC1L1
Activation of lipoprotein lipase through PPAR-alpha
Direct removal of LDL particles by the kidneys

questions.explanation: Answer: more LDL receptors on liver cells. Why: statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that turns HMG-CoA into mevalonate in cholesterol synthesis. With less cholesterol made inside the liver, liver cells put more LDL receptors on their surface and pull more LDL out of the blood. Main adverse effects are muscle problems (myalgia, myopathy, and rarely rhabdomyolysis) and liver enzyme elevation.

whyWrong.b: Binding bile acids in the gut is how bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colesevelam) work.
whyWrong.c: Blocking the Niemann-Pick C1-like 1 (NPC1L1) cholesterol transporter in the intestine is how ezetimibe works.
whyWrong.d: PPAR-alpha activation, which upregulates lipoprotein lipase, is the mechanism of fibrates, which mainly lower triglycerides.
whyWrong.e: LDL is cleared by the liver through LDL receptors, not by the kidneys.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department confused after drinking from a container in his garage. Serum sodium is 140 mEq/L, chloride 102 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 10 mEq/L. Measured serum osmolality is 330 mOsm/kg, and the calculated osmolality is 290 mOsm/kg. Serum creatinine rises over the next day, and urine microscopy shows calcium oxalate crystals.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's kidney injury?

options.text: Deposition of calcium oxalate in the renal tubules
Formic acid injury to the renal tubules

questions.explanation: Answer: calcium oxalate deposition. Why: this is ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning. Show the math: anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3) = 140 - (102 + 10) = 28, which is high (normal is roughly 8 to 12). Osmolal gap = measured - calculated = 330 - 290 = 40, also high, because the unmetabolized alcohol is osmotically active. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethylene glycol to glycolic acid (the main cause of the acidosis) and eventually oxalic acid, which binds calcium and deposits in the proximal tubules, causing acute kidney injury. Fomepizole, which blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, is the antidote.

whyWrong.b: Formic acid is the toxic metabolite of methanol, which classically damages the retina and causes vision loss, not oxalate crystals.
whyWrong.c: Acetone comes from isopropyl alcohol, which raises the osmolal gap but does not cause a high anion gap acidosis.
whyWrong.d: Nothing suggests muscle injury, and myoglobin would not explain an osmolal gap or oxalate crystals.
whyWrong.e: Starvation ketosis causes a mild anion gap acidosis without a large osmolal gap or oxalate crystals.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man notices cola-colored urine on the second day of a sore throat and runny nose. He had a similar episode with a cold last year. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows red blood cells and red blood cell casts with mild proteinuria. A renal biopsy is performed.
questions.leadIn: Immunofluorescence microscopy is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Granular IgA deposits in the mesangium
Linear IgG deposits along the glomerular basement membrane
Granular IgG and C3 deposits in a 'starry sky' pattern
Granular IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q deposits

questions.explanation: Answer: granular mesangial IgA. Why: blood in the urine that starts during (or right after) an upper respiratory infection, and recurs, is IgA nephropathy (Berger disease), the most common glomerulonephritis. Abnormal galactose-deficient IgA1 forms immune complexes that lodge in the mesangium. C3 often deposits alongside the IgA, while C1q is usually absent.

whyWrong.b: Linear IgG along the basement membrane is anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome), often with lung hemorrhage.
whyWrong.c: Granular IgG and C3 'starry sky' is poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which appears 1 to 3 weeks after the infection, not during it.
whyWrong.d: No deposits fits minimal change disease or pauci-immune vasculitis, not hematuria during an infection.
whyWrong.e: This 'full house' pattern, including C1q, is typical of lupus nephritis.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman who works on a sheep farm develops fever, chills, severe headache, fatigue, and muscle aches 3 weeks after helping with the spring lambing. She has a dry cough. She has no rash and does not recall any tick or insect bites. Serologic testing confirms Coxiella burnetii infection.
questions.leadIn: This patient most likely acquired the infection by which of the following routes?

options.text: Inhaling dust contaminated with birth products of infected animals
Respiratory droplets from an infected coworker

questions.explanation: Answer: inhaling contaminated dust. Why: Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever. People are infected by breathing in dust contaminated with the birth products, urine, feces, or milk of infected goats, sheep, and cattle, so lambing and calving season is high risk. Illness is flu-like (fever, chills, fatigue, muscle pain). A small number of people develop chronic Q fever, and having heart valve disease raises that risk.

whyWrong.b: Tick-borne rickettsial diseases such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever typically cause a rash; this patient has none and recalls no bite, and her exposure is to birthing sheep.
whyWrong.c: Undercooked pork transmits Trichinella and Taenia solium, not this infection.
whyWrong.d: Mosquitoes transmit malaria and arboviruses, which do not fit this farm exposure.
whyWrong.e: Person-to-person spread is not how Q fever is acquired; the source is infected animals.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has a large, painful skin abscess on his thigh. Culture of the drainage grows gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase positive and coagulase positive. The isolate is resistant to oxacillin and to all cephalosporins tested but is susceptible to vancomycin.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this organism's resistance to oxacillin?

options.text: Production of an altered penicillin-binding protein encoded by mecA
Production of a penicillinase that hydrolyzes oxacillin
Substitution of D-alanyl-D-lactate in cell wall precursors
Loss of outer membrane porin channels
Methylation of the 23S ribosomal RNA binding site

questions.explanation: Answer: altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) from the mecA gene. Why: this is methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Beta-lactam drugs kill bacteria by binding penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), the enzymes that cross-link the cell wall. MRSA carries mecA, which makes PBP2a, a PBP that beta-lactams cannot effectively block, so the cell keeps building its wall. That is why MRSA is resistant to essentially all beta-lactams and is treated with drugs like vancomycin.

whyWrong.b: Oxacillin and methicillin were designed to resist staphylococcal penicillinase, so penicillinase does not explain oxacillin resistance.
whyWrong.c: Replacing D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac is how enterococci resist vancomycin, and this isolate is vancomycin susceptible.
whyWrong.d: Porin loss is a resistance mechanism of gram-negative bacteria, which have an outer membrane; staphylococci do not.
whyWrong.e: 23S rRNA methylation causes resistance to macrolides and clindamycin, not to beta-lactams.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has had high fever and cough for 3 days. He is coughing up thick, dark red, jelly-like sputum. Chest x-ray shows dense consolidation of the right upper lobe.
questions.leadIn: A Gram stain of the sputum is most likely to show which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: encapsulated gram-negative rods. Why: 'currant jelly' sputum with upper lobe pneumonia in a person with alcohol use disorder (or diabetes) is classic for Klebsiella pneumoniae. It is a gram-negative, non-motile, encapsulated rod, and its polysaccharide capsule is its most important virulence factor.

whyWrong.b: Lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci are Streptococcus pneumoniae, which classically causes rust-colored sputum.
whyWrong.c: Gram-positive cocci in clusters are Staphylococcus aureus, which can cause pneumonia (often after influenza) but not currant jelly sputum.
whyWrong.d: Small gram-negative coccobacilli fit Haemophilus influenzae, a common cause of pneumonia in COPD, without currant jelly sputum.
whyWrong.e: Gram-negative diplococci are Neisseria or Moraxella; Moraxella causes bronchitis in COPD, not this picture.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has had slowly worsening shortness of breath and a dry cough for 18 months. He has fine 'Velcro-like' crackles at both lung bases and clubbing of the fingers. High-resolution CT shows reticular opacities and honeycombing at the lung bases.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following pulmonary function test patterns is most likely?

options.text: Normal FEV1/FVC ratio and decreased total lung capacity
Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio and increased total lung capacity
Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio and decreased total lung capacity
Normal FEV1/FVC ratio and increased total lung capacity
Normal FEV1/FVC ratio and normal total lung capacity

questions.explanation: Answer: normal FEV1/FVC with low total lung capacity (TLC). Why: this is pulmonary fibrosis, a restrictive lung disease. Stiff lungs cannot fill fully, so TLC and FVC (forced vital capacity) fall. FEV1 (air blown out in 1 second) falls about as much as FVC, so the FEV1/FVC ratio stays normal (above 0.70). A restrictive pattern is defined by a normal ratio with TLC below 80% of predicted. An obstructive pattern is the opposite: FEV1/FVC below 0.70, often with air trapping.

whyWrong.b: A low ratio with high TLC is obstructive disease with hyperinflation, such as emphysema.
whyWrong.c: A low ratio means obstruction; combined with low TLC it suggests a mixed defect, which does not fit isolated fibrosis.
whyWrong.d: High TLC means air trapping or hyperinflation, the opposite of a stiff fibrotic lung.
whyWrong.e: With honeycombing and crackles, lung volumes would not be normal.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man has had very itchy skin for 2 months and now has many large, tense blisters on his inner thighs, groin, and lower abdomen. Rubbing normal-looking skin next to a blister does not cause it to peel. His mouth is not involved. Biopsy shows a subepidermal blister with many eosinophils.
questions.leadIn: Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone
Net-like (chicken-wire) IgG between keratinocytes in the epidermis
IgE bound to dermal mast cells only
Granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae

questions.explanation: Answer: linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane. Why: tense, itchy blisters in an elderly patient with a negative Nikolsky sign and a subepidermal split with eosinophils is bullous pemphigoid. Autoantibodies target hemidesmosome proteins BP180 and BP230, which anchor the epidermis to the basement membrane, so antibody and complement line up along the basement membrane zone. Because the split is below the epidermis, the blister roof is thick and the blisters are tense.

whyWrong.b: A net-like intraepidermal pattern is pemphigus vulgaris, caused by antibodies to desmogleins 1 and 3. It shows suprabasal acantholysis ('tombstone' basal cells), a positive Nikolsky sign, easily ruptured blisters, and first appears in the mouth in about 80% of cases, with skin blisters following.
whyWrong.c: Bullous pemphigoid is antibody mediated, so deposits are expected.
whyWrong.d: IgE on mast cells is type I hypersensitivity (hives), which does not form subepidermal blisters.
whyWrong.e: Granular IgA in the dermal papillae is dermatitis herpetiformis, the itchy, grouped-vesicle rash linked to celiac disease.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman receives a kidney transplant. Her maintenance immunosuppression includes a drug that is a prodrug of mycophenolic acid. Over the next months she has frequent diarrhea, and her leukocyte count falls to 3,200/mm3.
questions.leadIn: This drug suppresses lymphocyte proliferation by inhibiting which of the following?

options.text: Thymidylate synthase via incorporation of a fluorinated pyrimidine

questions.explanation: Answer: inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH). Why: mycophenolate mofetil is converted to mycophenolic acid, which inhibits IMPDH and blocks the de novo pathway for making guanosine nucleotides. Proliferating lymphocytes are starved of guanine nucleotides and cannot divide. Common adverse effects are GI upset (especially diarrhea) and low blood counts (leukopenia). The boxed warning lists pregnancy loss and birth defects, lymphoma and skin cancer, and serious infections.

whyWrong.b: Calcineurin inhibition (blocking IL-2 transcription) is the mechanism of tacrolimus and cyclosporine, which are nephrotoxic.
whyWrong.c: mTOR inhibition (blocking the response to IL-2) is the mechanism of sirolimus and everolimus.
whyWrong.d: Dihydrofolate reductase inhibition is the mechanism of methotrexate.
whyWrong.e: Thymidylate synthase inhibition via a fluorinated pyrimidine is 5-fluorouracil, a chemotherapy drug, not a transplant immunosuppressant.

sources.title: FDA prescribing information: CellCept (mycophenolate mofetil), via DailyMed

questions.stem: In a randomized controlled trial, 2000 adults with atrial fibrillation receive either a new anticoagulant or placebo for 5 years. Stroke occurs in 100 of 1000 patients (10%) in the placebo group and in 60 of 1000 patients (6%) in the drug group.
questions.leadIn: How many patients must be treated with the new drug for 5 years to prevent one stroke?
questions.explanation: Answer: 25. Why: number needed to treat (NNT) = 1 / absolute risk reduction (ARR). ARR = control event rate - treatment event rate = 0.10 - 0.06 = 0.04. NNT = 1 / 0.04 = 25. (If the answer is not a whole number, round up.) For comparison, relative risk (RR) = 0.06 / 0.10 = 0.6, and relative risk reduction (RRR) = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4, or 40%.

whyWrong.b: 17 comes from 1 / 0.06, which uses the treatment group's event rate instead of the difference between groups.
whyWrong.c: 10 comes from 1 / 0.10, which uses the placebo group's event rate instead of the difference.
whyWrong.d: 40 is the relative risk reduction expressed as a percentage, not the NNT.
whyWrong.e: 3 comes from 1 / 0.4, which wrongly uses the relative risk reduction instead of the absolute risk reduction.

sources.title: Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (Oxford): Number Needed to Treat (NNT)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old right-handed man has sudden weakness of his right arm. When asked to smile, the right corner of his mouth droops. He can wrinkle his forehead and close both eyes tightly on both sides.
questions.leadIn: A lesion at which of the following sites best explains his facial findings?

options.text: Right facial nerve in the facial canal
Left facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen
Right facial nucleus in the pons

questions.explanation: Answer: left corticobulbar tract (an upper motor neuron lesion). Why: weakness of only the lower face on the side opposite the lesion, with the forehead spared, means an upper motor neuron (central) lesion. The forehead muscles receive input from both sides of the brain, so one damaged side cannot paralyze them. Damage at or below the facial nucleus (a lower motor neuron lesion, such as Bell palsy) weakens the whole face on the same side, forehead included. The right arm weakness also points to the left hemisphere.

whyWrong.b: A right facial nerve lesion would weaken the whole right face, including the forehead.
whyWrong.c: A left facial nerve lesion would weaken the whole left face, not the right lower face.
whyWrong.d: A right cortical lesion would cause left-sided weakness.
whyWrong.e: A facial nucleus lesion is a lower motor neuron lesion and would weaken the entire face on the same side, forehead included.

sources.title: StatPearls: Neuroanatomy, Lower Motor Neuron Lesion

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is admitted with a large anterior myocardial infarction. Six hours later he becomes confused. Blood pressure is 78/50 mm Hg and pulse is 118/min. His hands and feet are cold and clammy, and there are crackles over both lung fields. A pulmonary artery catheter is placed.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following sets of measurements is most likely?

options.text: Low cardiac index, high pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
Low cardiac index, low pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
High cardiac index, low pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
Normal cardiac index, normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
Normal cardiac index, high pulmonary capillary wedge pressure

questions.explanation: Answer: low cardiac index with high wedge pressure. Why: this is cardiogenic shock, and acute MI is its most common cause. The damaged left ventricle cannot pump, so cardiac output falls (cardiac index 2.2 L/min/m2 or less) and blood backs up into the lungs, raising the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP, above 15 mm Hg) and causing crackles. A PCWP above 15 mm Hg separates cardiogenic from non-cardiogenic shock. The body responds with sympathetic vasoconstriction, which is why the skin is cold and clammy.

whyWrong.b: Low output with a low wedge pressure fits hypovolemic shock: the problem is too little blood volume, not a failing pump, so filling pressure is low (PCWP 15 mm Hg or less means non-cardiogenic) and the lungs are clear.
whyWrong.c: High output with a low wedge pressure fits distributive (e.g., septic) shock, where the primary problem is low peripheral vascular resistance, not pump failure.
whyWrong.d: Normal values would not explain hypotension, confusion, and pulmonary congestion.
whyWrong.e: A normal cardiac index would not explain hypotension and poor perfusion after a large MI; low output (cardiac index 2.2 L/min/m2 or less) is what defines cardiogenic shock.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had three calcium-containing kidney stones in 2 years. A 24-hour urine collection shows high urinary calcium. Her serum calcium and parathyroid hormone are normal. Her physician prescribes a diuretic to reduce urinary calcium excretion.
questions.leadIn: This drug most likely acts by inhibiting which of the following?

options.text: Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
Carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
Aldosterone receptor in the collecting duct
Water reabsorption by acting as an osmotic agent

questions.explanation: Answer: the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Why: thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone) block this transporter and increase calcium reabsorption, which lowers urine calcium and helps prevent calcium stones. Because of this, thiazides can cause high serum calcium. Other key thiazide side effects are low potassium, low sodium, high uric acid (gout), high glucose, and high lipids.

whyWrong.b: Loop diuretics (furosemide) block Na-K-2Cl in the thick ascending limb, which also causes calcium and magnesium loss in the urine, the opposite of what she needs.
whyWrong.c: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide) alkalinize the urine, which favors calcium phosphate stones, and do not lower urine calcium.
whyWrong.d: Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) are potassium-sparing diuretics and are not used to lower urine calcium.
whyWrong.e: Osmotic diuretics (mannitol) are used for raised intracranial pressure, not to prevent kidney stones.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus has had vomiting for 2 days and is now breathing deeply and rapidly. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.26, PaCO2 23 mm Hg, HCO3 10 mEq/L. Serum sodium is 140 mEq/L and chloride is 100 mEq/L.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes this patient's acid-base status?

options.text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with a concurrent respiratory acidosis
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with a concurrent respiratory alkalosis
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Primary respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation

questions.explanation: Answer: high anion gap metabolic acidosis (from diabetic ketoacidosis) with appropriate compensation and no second disorder. Show the math: pH is low and HCO3 is low, so the primary problem is metabolic acidosis. Anion gap (AG) = Na - (Cl + HCO3) = 140 - (100 + 10) = 30, high (normal about 8 to 12). Winters formula: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 +/- 2 = 1.5 x 10 + 8 = 23, range 21 to 25. Measured PaCO2 is 23, so the lungs compensated exactly as expected.

whyWrong.b: A concurrent respiratory acidosis would leave PaCO2 above the Winters range (above 25).
whyWrong.c: A concurrent respiratory alkalosis would push PaCO2 below the Winters range (below 21).
whyWrong.d: The anion gap is 30, which is high, not normal.
whyWrong.e: The pH is low (acidemia), so the primary disorder cannot be an alkalosis.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anion Gap and Non-Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has had repeated vomiting for 1 week from a gastric outlet obstruction. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.50, PaCO2 46 mm Hg, HCO3 34 mEq/L.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes this patient's acid-base status?

options.text: Metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Metabolic alkalosis with a concurrent respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis with a concurrent respiratory alkalosis

questions.explanation: Answer: metabolic alkalosis, appropriately compensated. Why: vomiting removes stomach acid, so HCO3 rises and the pH goes up. The lungs compensate by breathing less to hold on to CO2. Show the math: expected PaCO2 = 40 + 0.6 x (HCO3 - 24) = 40 + 0.6 x (34 - 24) = 46, which matches the measured value. (Some review books use about 0.7 instead of 0.6; both are approximate.)

whyWrong.b: The high PaCO2 is exactly what compensation predicts (46), so it is not a second respiratory acidosis. This is the classic trap.
whyWrong.c: A concurrent respiratory alkalosis would make PaCO2 lower than expected, not 46.
whyWrong.d: Respiratory acidosis would make the pH low; this pH is high.
whyWrong.e: Respiratory alkalosis would make PaCO2 low; here it is high.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has had profuse watery diarrhea for 4 days. Serum sodium is 138 mEq/L, chloride is 114 mEq/L, and bicarbonate is 14 mEq/L. Arterial pH is 7.30.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes this patient's anion gap and type of acidosis?

options.text: 10 mEq/L; normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
24 mEq/L; high anion gap metabolic acidosis
10 mEq/L; high anion gap metabolic acidosis
38 mEq/L; high anion gap metabolic acidosis
24 mEq/L; normal anion gap metabolic acidosis

questions.explanation: Answer: anion gap 10, normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis. Show the math: AG = Na - (Cl + HCO3) = 138 - (114 + 14) = 10, inside the normal 8 to 12. Why: stool is rich in bicarbonate, and chloride rises to replace the lost bicarbonate, so the gap stays normal. Diarrhea and renal tubular acidosis are the main causes of normal anion gap acidosis.

whyWrong.b: 24 is Na - Cl only; it forgets to subtract HCO3.
whyWrong.c: An anion gap of 10 is normal, not high.
whyWrong.d: 38 comes from adding HCO3 instead of subtracting it.
whyWrong.e: 24 is Na - Cl only, and a gap of 24 would be high, not normal.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anion Gap and Non-Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with long-standing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) comes for a routine visit. He feels at his baseline. His arterial PaCO2 has been stable at 60 mm Hg for months.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following serum bicarbonate concentrations is most consistent with appropriate compensation?
questions.explanation: Answer: about 32 mEq/L. Why: this is chronic respiratory acidosis, and over days the kidneys retain about 4 mEq/L of HCO3 for every 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO2. Show the math: PaCO2 is 20 above 40, so HCO3 = 24 + 2 x 4 = 32.

whyWrong.b: 26 uses the acute rule (+1 per 10 mm Hg). Using it here would make a normal COPD gas look like an added metabolic alkalosis.
whyWrong.c: 24 means no compensation at all, which does not fit months of stable CO2 retention.
whyWrong.d: A low HCO3 would mean a concurrent metabolic acidosis.
whyWrong.e: 40 is more than compensation predicts and would suggest an added metabolic alkalosis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after taking a large number of aspirin tablets. She has ringing in her ears and is breathing fast. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.47, PaCO2 20 mm Hg, HCO3 14 mEq/L. Serum sodium is 140 mEq/L and chloride is 102 mEq/L.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes this patient's acid-base status?

options.text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis and primary respiratory alkalosis
Primary respiratory alkalosis with appropriate metabolic compensation only
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation only
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis and primary respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis and primary respiratory acidosis

questions.explanation: Answer: mixed disorder, high anion gap metabolic acidosis plus primary respiratory alkalosis. Why: salicylates stimulate the brain's breathing center (respiratory alkalosis) and also add acid (metabolic acidosis). Show the math: AG = 140 - (102 + 14) = 24, high. If the acidosis were alone, Winters predicts PaCO2 = 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29 +/- 2 (27 to 31). The measured PaCO2 of 20 is far lower, so there is extra hyperventilation: a second, primary respiratory alkalosis.

whyWrong.b: A pure respiratory alkalosis would not create a high anion gap of 24.
whyWrong.c: PaCO2 of 20 is well below the Winters range of 27 to 31, so compensation alone does not explain it. The near-normal pH is the trap.
whyWrong.d: The anion gap is 24, which is high, not normal.
whyWrong.e: HCO3 is low, not high, and PaCO2 is low, not high.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anion Gap and Non-Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man who emigrated from a country with high tuberculosis rates has had 2 months of cough, night sweats, low-grade fevers, and a 6-kg weight loss. He had a positive tuberculin skin test years ago that was never treated. He recently started high-dose prednisone for another condition. Chest x-ray shows a cavitary lesion in the apex of the right upper lobe.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the location of this lesion?

options.text: Reactivation of latent infection, which favors the apical-posterior lung segments
Primary infection, which favors the middle and lower lung zones
Aspiration while unconscious, which favors dependent lung segments
Hematogenous spread from a distant site, which produces a single apical cavity
Progressive primary infection in an immunosuppressed host, which favors the lower lung zones

questions.explanation: Answer: reactivation (secondary) tuberculosis. Why: in someone with an old positive skin test, weakened immunity (here, high-dose steroids) lets latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis reactivate. Reactivation TB favors the apical-posterior segments of the upper lobes and often cavitates, because granulomas can undergo caseous necrosis and erode into an airway. M. tuberculosis is acid-fast because of the high lipid content of its cell wall, and culture is the gold standard for diagnosing active disease.

whyWrong.b: Primary TB usually causes an infiltrate in the middle and lower lung zones, not an apical cavity, and this patient was infected years ago.
whyWrong.c: Aspiration affects dependent segments and does not explain years of latent TB followed by reactivation on steroids.
whyWrong.d: Hematogenous (miliary) spread causes many tiny nodules throughout both lungs, not a single apical cavity.
whyWrong.e: In an immunocompromised person, a new (primary) infection can progress to pneumonia mainly in the lower lung zones. This patient was infected years ago and has an apical cavity, which points to reactivation.

questions.topic: Thyroid hormone synthesis and antithyroid drugs
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has heat intolerance, palpitations, weight loss, a diffuse goiter, and bulging eyes. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is high. She is started on methimazole. Two months later she develops fever and a severe sore throat, and her absolute neutrophil count is very low.
questions.leadIn: Methimazole lowers thyroid hormone production by inhibiting which of the following?

options.text: Release of stored hormone from thyroglobulin
Thyroid hormone receptors in target tissues

questions.explanation: Answer: thyroid peroxidase. Why: methimazole inhibits thyroid peroxidase, the enzyme that attaches iodine to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin and couples them to form T4 and T3. Her fever and sore throat with very low neutrophils is agranulocytosis, a serious adverse effect of methimazole. Methimazole is also avoided in the first trimester because of birth defects (e.g., aplasia cutis), while propylthiouracil (PTU) carries a risk of severe liver injury.

whyWrong.b: The sodium-iodide symporter carries iodide into thyroid cells; it is inhibited by perchlorate, not by methimazole.
whyWrong.c: Methimazole does not affect hormone already stored in the thyroid. It blocks new synthesis, so hormone levels fall only as the stored supply in thyroglobulin is used up.
whyWrong.d: Methimazole does not block the stimulating antibodies of Graves disease; it blocks hormone synthesis downstream of them.
whyWrong.e: Methimazole does not act on thyroid hormone receptors; beta-blockers are used to control symptoms at the tissue level.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has new hypertension of 168/104 mm Hg found at a routine visit. She does not smoke and has no family history of hypertension. A bruit is heard in the right upper abdomen. Renal angiography shows alternating narrowing and dilation of the middle portion of the right renal artery.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hypertension?
questions.explanation: Answer: fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD). Why: FMD most often affects women younger than 50, and onset of hypertension before age 30 strongly suggests it. It typically involves the middle and distal renal artery and gives a classic "string-of-beads" look on angiography. The narrowed artery lowers perfusion to that kidney, which releases renin and drives renovascular hypertension. In contrast, atherosclerosis causes about 90% of renovascular hypertension overall but affects older patients and the origin (first 2 cm) of the artery.

whyWrong.b: Atherosclerotic stenosis affects patients older than 45 and narrows the renal artery origin, not the middle segment in a beaded pattern.
whyWrong.c: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension with low renin and often low potassium, but not an abnormal renal angiogram.
whyWrong.d: Pheochromocytoma causes episodic headaches, sweating, and palpitations and would not explain a beaded renal artery.
whyWrong.e: Coarctation causes higher blood pressure in the arms than the legs with delayed femoral pulses, not a renal artery lesion.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with HIV infection and a CD4+ count of 90/mm3 has painful swallowing. Endoscopy shows white plaques on the esophageal mucosa, and biopsy shows yeast with pseudohyphae. He is started on oral fluconazole.
questions.leadIn: This drug acts by inhibiting which of the following?

options.text: Beta-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase in the cell wall
Fungal RNA synthesis after conversion to 5-fluorouracil
Membrane integrity by binding ergosterol and forming pores

questions.explanation: Answer: lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase. Why: azoles such as fluconazole inhibit this enzyme, a key step in making ergosterol, the main sterol of fungal cell membranes. Without ergosterol the membrane does not work properly. Esophageal candidiasis in advanced HIV is commonly treated with fluconazole.

whyWrong.b: Inhibiting beta-glucan synthase is the mechanism of echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin).
whyWrong.c: Inhibiting squalene epoxidase is the mechanism of terbinafine, used for nail and skin fungal infections.
whyWrong.d: Conversion to 5-fluorouracil, which interferes with fungal RNA synthesis, is the mechanism of flucytosine.
whyWrong.e: Binding ergosterol to form membrane pores is the mechanism of amphotericin B, which is nephrotoxic.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy has had a runny nose and low-grade fever for 2 days. Tonight he developed a barking, seal-like cough and a high-pitched noise when breathing in. He is not drooling and is not toxic appearing. A neck x-ray shows narrowing of the airway just below the vocal cords.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Answer: parainfluenza virus. Why: a barking cough and inspiratory stridor after cold symptoms in a toddler is croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), most commonly caused by parainfluenza viruses. It occurs from 6 months to 6 years of age, peaking between 1 and 2 years. Subglottic narrowing produces the "steeple sign" on x-ray.

whyWrong.b: RSV is the most common cause of bronchiolitis in children 2 years and younger, which causes diffuse wheezing across both lungs rather than a barking cough and stridor.
whyWrong.c: Hib causes epiglottitis: drooling, difficulty swallowing, and a child sitting in a tripod position. Epiglottitis is rare in vaccinated children.
whyWrong.d: Group A strep causes pharyngitis and can cause peritonsillar abscess, not subglottic narrowing with a barking cough.
whyWrong.e: Diphtheria causes a thick gray membrane over the tonsils and pharynx, and it has become rare where children receive diphtheria toxoid vaccine.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man has a positive guaiac-based fecal occult blood test on routine screening. He has no GI symptoms. Colonoscopy is completely normal. He mentions that he ate steak several times in the days before collecting the samples.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the positive guaiac test?

options.text: Peroxidase activity of heme from dietary red meat
Cross-reactivity of the test with human globin from upper GI bleeding only
Antibodies to human hemoglobin binding animal hemoglobin

questions.explanation: Answer: peroxidase activity of heme from red meat. Why: the guaiac test detects the pseudoperoxidase activity of heme, which turns the guaiac reagent blue. It cannot tell human heme from animal heme, so red meat (and raw fruits and vegetables rich in peroxidases) can cause false positives. The fecal immunochemical test (FIT) detects human globin, needs no diet changes, and is more specific for lower GI bleeding.

whyWrong.b: Detecting human globin is how FIT works, not guaiac tests, and globin from upper GI bleeding is mostly digested.
whyWrong.c: Large doses of vitamin C cause false-negative guaiac results, not false positives.
whyWrong.d: Guaiac tests use a chemical reaction, not antibodies; antibody-based testing is FIT, which is specific to human globin.
whyWrong.e: Bilirubin breakdown products do not have peroxidase activity and do not cause positive guaiac tests.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with severe osteoarthritis needs long-term high-dose NSAID therapy. He had a bleeding gastric ulcer 2 years ago. His physician adds a drug to reduce his risk of another NSAID-induced ulcer. A few days later he develops loose stools.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes the added drug?

options.text: Prostaglandin E1 analog that increases gastric mucus and bicarbonate secretion
Proton pump inhibitor that irreversibly blocks the H+/K+ ATPase
Agent that forms a protective coat over ulcer bases in acid

questions.explanation: Answer: misoprostol, a prostaglandin E1 analog. Why: prostaglandins made by COX-1 help protect the stomach lining, which NSAIDs undermine. Misoprostol replaces that protection: it increases mucus and bicarbonate secretion and reduces acid secretion, lowering the risk of NSAID-induced ulcers. Diarrhea is one of its most common adverse effects. It should not be used for this purpose in pregnancy because it can cause abortion, premature birth, and birth defects.

whyWrong.b: PPIs (e.g., omeprazole) also prevent NSAID ulcers, but they cause diarrhea less often, and they act by blocking the proton pump, not by replacing prostaglandins.
whyWrong.c: H2 blockers (e.g., famotidine) reduce acid secretion but do not replace prostaglandins.
whyWrong.d: Sucralfate breaks apart in stomach acid and binds the mucosa to form a protective layer. It is not a prostaglandin, and its most common side effect is constipation rather than diarrhea.
whyWrong.e: Antacids neutralize acid that is already in the stomach; they do not replace prostaglandins.

questions.topic: Acute mental status change in the elderly
questions.stem: An 84-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because she has been confused since yesterday. Her daughter says she was living independently and managing her own finances last week. Today she is drowsy one hour and agitated the next, cannot keep track of a conversation, and cannot recite the months backward. She has a temperature of 38.2°C (100.8°F) and dysuria. Urinalysis shows many leukocytes and nitrites.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: delirium. Why: delirium develops acutely and fluctuates in severity, and its core feature is inattention (here, losing track of conversation and failing months-backward) with a fluctuating level of consciousness. Urinary tract infection is a common trigger in older adults, as are anticholinergic drugs and benzodiazepines. Delirium is often reversible when the cause is treated. Dementia, by contrast, develops gradually, and patients are usually awake and alert with fixed deficits.

whyWrong.b: Alzheimer disease, like other dementias, is a slow, chronic, progressive decline. It does not appear overnight with a fluctuating level of alertness.
whyWrong.c: Severe depression can mimic dementia (pseudodementia), but it does not explain an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention that began with a fever.
whyWrong.d: Vascular dementia comes from cumulative strokes and small vessel damage and is a chronic decline. Fever with a urinary infection and a one-day change point to delirium.
whyWrong.e: Fluctuating cognition is a core feature of Lewy body dementia and can mimic delirium, but it is a chronic dementia, and this patient was fully independent a week ago.

sources.title: StatPearls: Differentiating Delirium Versus Dementia in Older Adults

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has a painful band of vesicles on the left side of her chest in one dermatome. She is treated with famciclovir, a prodrug that is converted to penciclovir. The drug inhibits viral replication in infected cells but has little effect on uninfected cells.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains this drug's selectivity for infected cells?

options.text: It is first phosphorylated by a virus-encoded thymidine kinase
It binds a viral surface glycoprotein to block entry
It is activated only by host cell kinases that are overexpressed in infected cells

questions.explanation: Answer: first phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase. Why: famciclovir is converted to penciclovir, which the herpesvirus thymidine kinase phosphorylates to a monophosphate. Uninfected cells cannot do this first step, so the drug is activated mainly in infected cells. Host enzymes then make the triphosphate, which inhibits herpesvirus DNA polymerase and terminates the growing DNA chain. Acyclovir is a related nucleoside analog that is also activated to a triphosphate and blocks viral DNA synthesis.

whyWrong.b: Blocking viral entry is how fusion inhibitors work: enfuvirtide is a peptide modeled on the HIV fusion protein gp41 that stops HIV from fusing with the cell. Herpes antivirals do not work this way.
whyWrong.c: Host kinases add the later phosphates, but the selective first step depends on the viral enzyme.
whyWrong.d: Neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir treat influenza A and B, not herpes zoster.
whyWrong.e: Protease inhibitors are used to treat HIV, not herpes zoster.

questions.topic: Primary biliary cholangitis vs primary sclerosing cholangitis
questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had 6 months of fatigue and generalized itching. She also has dry eyes and a dry mouth. She takes no medications, drinks no alcohol, and has no history of bowel disease. She is not jaundiced. Labs show alkaline phosphatase 410 U/L (normal 40-120), ALT 58 U/L (normal under 35), and total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL. Ultrasound shows no gallstones and no bile duct dilation.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). Why: about 95% of patients are women, usually aged 40 to 70. Itching and fatigue are common early symptoms (up to 80%), and dry mouth and eyes can come months or years before other symptoms; PBC is associated with Sjögren syndrome, systemic sclerosis, and autoimmune thyroiditis. Labs show a cholestatic pattern with a high alkaline phosphatase. Imaging is done first to exclude bile duct obstruction. The next test is antimitochondrial antibody (AMA), which is positive in 90-95%; serum IgM is also raised. Pathology: T cells destroy the small bile ducts inside the liver. Treatment: ursodeoxycholic acid. Contrast with PSC: mostly men, linked to ulcerative colitis, with "beaded" strictures of the large ducts.

whyWrong.b: PSC mostly affects men (60-71%), usually aged 25 to 45, is linked to ulcerative colitis in 60-80%, and shows multifocal strictures with a "beaded" appearance of the bile ducts inside and outside the liver.
whyWrong.c: Extrahepatic obstruction such as a common bile duct stone must be excluded with imaging; this ultrasound shows no stones and no dilated ducts.
whyWrong.d: Autoimmune hepatitis mainly injures hepatocytes and raises aminotransferases; overlap with autoimmune hepatitis is suspected when ALT is more than 5 times normal. Here ALT is only mildly raised and the pattern is cholestatic.
whyWrong.e: Drug-induced liver disease is on the list of cholestatic causes, but she takes no medications.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)

questions.stem: A trial compares survival with a new chemotherapy regimen versus standard therapy in patients with metastatic colon cancer, and the results are shown as Kaplan-Meier curves. One patient in the new-regimen group moved abroad 8 months after enrolling and was lost to follow-up. She was alive at her last visit.
questions.leadIn: How is this patient handled in the Kaplan-Meier analysis?

options.text: She counts as at risk until month 8, then is censored and leaves the risk set without being counted as a death
She is counted as a death at month 8
She is removed from the analysis entirely
She is counted as alive until the end of the study
She is assigned the median survival time of her group

questions.explanation: Answer: she is censored at month 8. Why: a Kaplan-Meier curve estimates the probability of surviving past each time point. A censored patient is one whose follow-up ended before an event; we know she survived at least to her last contact but not what happened after. She counts in the number at risk up to month 8 and then drops out of the risk set, so her data inform the curve without biasing it, as long as censoring is non-informative (her reason for leaving is unrelated to her prognosis). If sicker patients drop out more often, the curve overestimates survival. The curve steps down only at events (deaths). Median survival is read where the curve crosses 0.5 (50% surviving), and the log-rank test compares two curves.

whyWrong.b: The curve drops only at events. Counting a censored patient as a death would wrongly lower the survival estimate.
whyWrong.c: Removing her would waste real information: she is known to have survived at least 8 months, so she counts as at risk until then.
whyWrong.d: We do not know what happened after her last contact, so she cannot be assumed alive to the end of the study.
whyWrong.e: Kaplan-Meier analysis does not fill in guessed survival times; censored patients simply leave the risk set when follow-up ends.

sources.title: MedCalc Statistical Software Manual: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl is evaluated because she has not started puberty. She has female external genitalia, no breast development, and no pubic or axillary hair. Blood pressure is 165/100 mm Hg. Serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L, and she has a metabolic alkalosis. Karyotype is 46,XX. Serum deoxycorticosterone (DOC) and corticosterone are high, and sex steroids are low.
questions.leadIn: A deficiency of which of the following enzymes is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Answer: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency. Why: 17α-hydroxylase is needed to make cortisol and sex steroids. When it is blocked, precursors are pushed down the mineralocorticoid pathway, so DOC and corticosterone build up. DOC binds mineralocorticoid receptors and acts like aldosterone: hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Corticosterone has cortisol-like activity. Sex steroids are low, so puberty does not progress; the absence of puberty plus hypertension often leads to diagnosis in adolescence. Lab clues: high DOC and corticosterone, a high progesterone-to-17-hydroxyprogesterone ratio, and low sex steroids. Memory hook: of the CAH forms, two cause hypertension (17α and 11β); only 11β also causes androgen excess.

whyWrong.b: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes androgen excess that virilizes 46,XX infants, and about 75% of classic cases are salt wasting. It does not cause hypertension with absent puberty.
whyWrong.c: 11β-hydroxylase deficiency also causes hypertension and hypokalemia from DOC, but it causes androgen excess with early virilization, not absent puberty.
whyWrong.d: 3β-HSD deficiency blocks cortisol, aldosterone, and androgen synthesis, so it is a salt-wasting form of CAH, not a cause of hypertension.
whyWrong.e: StAR defects (lipoid CAH) present with adrenal insufficiency in early infancy and are a salt-wasting form of CAH, not a cause of hypertension.

questions.topic: Renal clearance and GFR (inulin vs creatinine)
questions.stem: In a renal physiology study, a healthy volunteer receives a continuous IV infusion of inulin. At steady state, urine flow is 2 mL/min, urine inulin concentration is 30 mg/mL, and plasma inulin concentration is 0.5 mg/mL. Creatinine clearance measured at the same time is 130 mL/min.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the best estimate of this person’s glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
questions.explanation: Answer: 120 mL/min. Why: clearance is the volume of plasma cleared of a substance per minute: C = (U × V) / P, where U is urine concentration, V is urine flow rate, and P is plasma concentration. Inulin clearance = (30 mg/mL × 2 mL/min) / 0.5 mg/mL = 120 mL/min. Inulin measures GFR accurately because it is freely filtered and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted. The same formula with para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) estimates renal plasma flow (RPF), and filtration fraction = GFR / RPF, normally about 20%.

whyWrong.b: Creatinine is also secreted by the tubules, so creatinine clearance overestimates GFR, especially when GFR is low. Inulin is the more accurate marker.
whyWrong.c: 60 is U / P (30 / 0.5), which leaves out the urine flow rate. Clearance is (U × V) / P.
whyWrong.d: 30 is U × V × P; the plasma concentration belongs in the denominator, not the numerator.
whyWrong.e: 7.5 is (U × P) / V, which swaps urine flow and plasma concentration. Clearance is (U × V) / P.

sources.title: LITFL Part One: Measurement of GFR (citing Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology)
StatPearls: Physiology, Renal Blood Flow and Filtration

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes is brought to the emergency department with polyuria and confusion. Serum sodium is 128 mEq/L and serum glucose is 700 mg/dL.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the best estimate of his serum sodium after correcting for the hyperglycemia?

options.text: It cannot be estimated without measuring plasma osmolality

questions.explanation: Answer: about 138 to 142 mEq/L, which is normal. Why: high glucose lowers the measured sodium. The most commonly used correction is 1.6 mEq/L for every 100 mg/dL rise in glucose. Glucose has risen about 600 mg/dL above normal (700 - 100), so 6 × 1.6 = 9.6, and the corrected sodium is 128 + 9.6 ≈ 138 mEq/L. Some sources use about 2.4 mEq/L per 100 mg/dL instead (Hillier 1999), especially when glucose is above about 440 mg/dL; that gives 128 + 14.4 ≈ 142 mEq/L. Either way, the corrected sodium is normal. Mechanism: glucose raises plasma osmolality and pulls water out of cells, diluting the sodium (translocational hyponatremia). As the glucose is treated, the water moves back into cells and the sodium rises. Do not confuse this with pseudohyponatremia, where severe hyperlipidemia or extreme hyperproteinemia (e.g., multiple myeloma) takes up space in the sample: the sodium in the serum itself and the osmolality are normal.

whyWrong.b: 128 is the measured value. The correction estimates what the sodium will be once the glucose, and the water it pulled out of cells, return to normal.
whyWrong.c: 134 adds only 1 mEq/L per 100 mg/dL. The factor is about 1.6 mEq/L per 100 mg/dL rise in glucose (or about 2.4 in some sources), not 1.
whyWrong.d: 118 subtracts the correction. Hyperglycemia lowers the measured sodium, so the correction is added.
whyWrong.e: No osmolality is needed: the correction is calculated from the glucose alone, at about 1.6 mEq/L for every 100 mg/dL rise.

sources.title: Huffman GB. Adjusting Sodium Levels in Patients with Hyperglycemia. Am Fam Physician 1999;60(6):1821 (summary of Hillier TA et al., Am J Med 1999;106:399-403)
